clue.text: Cab door being slammed in the city

indicators.note: something slammed is knocked about violently, so these letters are battered into a new order

blocks.note: the seven letters used as they stand

explanation.surface: A taxi door gets banged shut somewhere in town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the city' looks like a vague scene-setter, but it is the whole definition. Cordoba is a historic city in southern Spain (and one in Argentina).
explanation.definitionFit: Cordoba is a famous Andalusian urban centre with a great mosque-cathedral, so it is an example of a city.

clue.text: Easy task that keeps learner secure

indicators.note: to keep something is to hold it inside, so one piece sits within another

blocks.note: a cinch is something very easy to do
L for learner, as on a learner driver's plates

explanation.surface: A simple job that keeps a trainee safe in their post.
explanation.walkthrough: 'secure' reads like an adjective describing the learner, but it is a verb meaning to make certain. The L goes after the first letter of the easy task.
explanation.definitionFit: To clinch a deal or victory is to settle it decisively, the same as securing or nailing it down.

clue.text: Irish turning up to celebrate their 1916 event?

blocks.note: surface padding naming the people whose revolt is meant; it supplies no letters
first meaning: getting up or going upward
second meaning: the Easter revolt in Dublin against British rule in 1916

explanation.surface: Irish people gathering to commemorate their famous 1916 uprising.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turning up' suggests arriving at a celebration, but it means going upward. The Easter Rising of 1916 was an armed revolt in Dublin against British rule.
explanation.definitionFit: Getting up from bed or ascending is rising, and the 1916 Dublin revolt against British rule is known as the Easter Rising.

clue.text: Roofer may be working here as an act of generosity

blocks.note: first meaning: literally up on top of a building
second meaning: free, paid for by the establishment

explanation.surface: A tradesman doing repairs on a home turns out to be doing the job for free.
explanation.walkthrough: The roofer's workplace is literally on top of a building, while the idiom describes drinks or services given away free by a bar or business.
explanation.definitionFit: Something given free by a pub or shop is provided without charge, the establishment paying, which is a generous gesture.

clue.text: Check car before start of travel

indicators.note: one thing coming before another places them side by side in that order
the start of a word is its opening letter, so only that one is kept

blocks.note: Audi is a German car make
the opening letter of this word

explanation.surface: Give the vehicle a once-over before setting off on a journey.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads like advice on vehicle safety, but 'car' stands for a particular make.
explanation.definitionFit: An audit is an official inspection, especially of accounts, so as a verb it means to examine or check formally.

clue.text: Cold girl in charge of major sporting event

blocks.note: C for cold, as on a tap
a lass is a girl
IC is the abbreviation for in charge

explanation.surface: A frosty young woman is running a big tournament.
explanation.walkthrough: 'of' looks like a link but sits inside the definition. In Britain the Classics are the five big flat horse races such as the Derby.
explanation.definitionFit: In racing, the five most prestigious British flat races are the Classics, so a classic is a premier fixture in the sporting calendar.

clue.text: Abandon vermouth? Don't be silly!

blocks.note: to come off something, such as a drug, is to give it up
It is short for Italian vermouth, as in gin and It

explanation.surface: Someone told to give up their martini replies with scorn.
explanation.walkthrough: Gin and It is a British cocktail of gin and Italian (sweet) vermouth, which is where 'It' comes from.
explanation.definitionFit: The exclamation is a colloquial way of telling someone they are talking nonsense, the same as saying stop being ridiculous.

clue.text: A container slightly open

blocks.note: taken as written
a glass pot with a lid, for jam or pickles

explanation.surface: A lid left loose on a pot or box.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as one description of a vessel, but splits into the article plus a kind of container.
explanation.definitionFit: A door left ajar stands a little way open, not fully shut.

clue.text: Don't go so fast providing son with information

indicators.note: with means alongside, so one part is placed together with the next

blocks.note: S for son, as in genealogies
the lowdown is the inside information on something

explanation.surface: A parent tells their boy to ease up while briefing him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'providing' looks like part of the wordplay but is just a joining word here.
explanation.definitionFit: Telling someone to reduce speed or take things more gently is exactly asking them to decelerate.

clue.text: Gestures of respect German observes in the auditorium?

indicators.note: an auditorium is where an audience listens, so we go by what is heard rather than written

blocks.note: Kurt is a typical German man's name
to observe is to see

explanation.surface: A German man watches bows and bobs being made in a theatre.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Kurt sees', said aloud, matches the plural of a bob of respect. The theatre setting makes curtseys at a curtain call apt.
explanation.definitionFit: A curtsey is a woman's bob, bending the knees, made as a sign of deference, so these are respectful gestures.

clue.text: Small picture shows day when teachers get more training

definitions.text: day when teachers get more training

blocks.note: first meaning: a small map or picture set within a larger one

blocks.clueFragment: day when teachers get more training
blocks.note: second meaning: the British in-service training day, when schools close to pupils

explanation.surface: A little photo depicts a staff training day at school.
explanation.walkthrough: INSET stands for in-service education and training; British schools close to pupils on INSET days while staff attend courses.
explanation.definitionFit: An inset is a small image placed inside a bigger one, and an INSET day is the British name for a staff training day.

clue.text: Editor turning stingy leads to our sort of attitude

indicators.note: something turning faces the other way, so its letters run backwards
to lead to something is to go in front of it, so the parts are placed in sequence

blocks.note: ED is the standard abbreviation for editor
mean means miserly
taken as written

explanation.surface: A newspaper boss growing miserly sets the tone for the whole office.
explanation.walkthrough: 'our' is used literally and sits at the end; the surface makes it sound like part of a phrase about our attitude.
explanation.definitionFit: Demeanour is outward behaviour or bearing, the manner a person shows, which is close to their attitude.

clue.text: Happy at home about nothing? There's argument

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece wraps another

blocks.note: content means satisfied, happy
someone at home is in
O looks like zero, nothing

explanation.surface: Someone is perfectly happy at home over nothing in particular, yet a row breaks out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'at home' is the crossword IN, and 'about' wraps it round the nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: Contention is disagreement or dispute, as in a bone of contention, so it is a synonym for argument.

clue.text: Some modest poetry

indicators.note: some means only part of, so the letters are a portion of the next word

blocks.note: the middle four letters of this word

explanation.surface: A small, unassuming collection of verse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'modest' reads as describing the poetry but holds the answer inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Odes are lyric poems, often addressed to a subject, so a set of them is poetry; the plural matches a mass noun loosely.

clue.text: This writer lacked a single bit of inspiration? You surprise me!

blocks.note: the setter speaking of themself is I
to lack something is to have none of it
one idea is a single spark of inspiration

explanation.surface: A writer with block is told something astonishing.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay is a whole sentence describing a blank writer, which turns out to be the same words as an exclamation of surprise.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying that you were unaware of something is a common response expressing astonishment at news.

clue.text: Unusual demand that you let me through?

definitions.text: demand that you let me through
definitions.note: a whole exclamation, 'Out of the way!'

blocks.note: first meaning: remote or uncommon, off the beaten track

blocks.clueFragment: demand that you let me through
blocks.note: second meaning: the shout of someone pushing past a crowd

explanation.surface: An odd request made by someone wanting to get past.
explanation.walkthrough: As an adjective the phrase means remote or out of the ordinary; shouted, it orders people to move aside.
explanation.definitionFit: Something remote or rarely encountered is out of the ordinary, and the exclamation tells bystanders to step aside.

clue.text: Not keeping up to date with rent's said to be bad

indicators.note: bad letters are ones that have gone wrong, so they are rearranged

blocks.note: the nine letters used as they stand

explanation.surface: A tenant behind on payments hears the rent is too much.
explanation.walkthrough: 'said' looks like a sound indicator but is just fodder; 'up to date with rent' seems one phrase, but the definition ends at 'date'.
explanation.definitionFit: Tardiness is lateness or slowness, failing to be on time, so it means not keeping pace with schedules.

clue.text: Present opportunities are in store here

definitions.text: Present opportunities are in store here

blocks.clueFragment: Present opportunities are in store here
blocks.note: surface reading: chances available now lie ahead in this place

blocks.clueFragment: Present opportunities are in store here
blocks.note: setter's reading: a retail outlet where presents can be bought

explanation.walkthrough: 'Present' looks like an adjective meaning current, and 'in store' like 'awaiting'; read instead as a noun for a gift and a literal shop.
explanation.definitionFit: A retail outlet selling souvenirs and presents is a store where chances to buy gifts are found.

clue.text: Co-operate in drama and dance

indicators.note: and adds one thing to another, so the parts are joined in order

blocks.note: a play is a drama
a ball is a formal dance

explanation.surface: Performers work together in a stage show with dancing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' looks like part of the surface phrase but just joins the definition to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: To play ball is an idiom for agreeing to work together or comply with what others want.

clue.text: Given pictures — dullest art, I fancy

indicators.note: fancy means elaborately decorated or imagined, so these letters are worked into a new pattern

blocks.note: the eleven letters used as they stand

explanation.surface: Someone shown paintings judges them the most boring art they can imagine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fancy' at the end looks like 'I imagine', but it signals the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: A book that is illustrated has been supplied with drawings or images, so it has been furnished with artwork.

clue.text: Payment demanded for stored electricity?

blocks.note: first meaning: a fee asked for
second meaning: the energy held in a battery

explanation.surface: A bill arrives for the power in your batteries.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads like one electricity bill, but the two halves are separate meanings of a single word.
explanation.definitionFit: A fee levied for a service is a charge, and the electrical energy accumulated in a battery is also called its charge.

clue.text: Difficult feature of card game ending in controversy

indicators.note: the ending of a word is its final letter, so only that one is kept

blocks.note: in games like bridge and whist each round of cards played is a trick
the final letter of this word

explanation.surface: A hard aspect of a card game ends in a row at the table.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ending in' sounds like a game finishing in argument, but it picks out one letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Something tricky is awkward or hard to handle, requiring care or skill, so it means difficult.

clue.text: Fiddles -- prime requirements for the orchestra, you suspect

indicators.note: prime means first, so the opening letter of each following word is needed

blocks.note: the opening letters of these four words

explanation.surface: Violins are, you'd guess, the basic needs of any orchestra.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fiddles' wants to be violins, given the orchestra; it is the verb, as in fiddles with something idly.
explanation.definitionFit: To toy with something is to play or meddle with it absent-mindedly, as one fiddles with a pen.

clue.text: Older sibling who keeps an unwelcome eye on you?

definitions.text: who keeps an unwelcome eye on you

blocks.note: first meaning: an elder male sibling

blocks.clueFragment: who keeps an unwelcome eye on you
blocks.note: second meaning: the all-seeing ruler in Orwell's Nineteen Eighty-Four, now any intrusive surveillance authority

explanation.surface: An elder brother who annoyingly watches over you.
explanation.walkthrough: In Orwell's novel posters warn that Big Brother is watching you; the term now means intrusive state surveillance.
explanation.definitionFit: A male sibling born earlier is literally one, and Orwell's surveillance figure gave the phrase its sinister watching sense.

clue.text: Victims of ridicule making objections audible

indicators.note: audible means able to be heard, so we work from a spoken sound

blocks.note: buts are objections, as in no ifs or buts

explanation.surface: People mocked by others start raising their complaints out loud.
explanation.walkthrough: The butt of a joke is the person laughed at; the objection word has one T but sounds the same.
explanation.definitionFit: The butt of a joke or of ridicule is its target, so the plural means those who are mocked.

clue.text: Celebrity in tabloid?

blocks.note: first meaning: a famous person
second meaning: the title of a popular British red-top daily newspaper

explanation.surface: A famous name appears in a gossip paper.
explanation.walkthrough: The Daily Star is a British tabloid newspaper, which supplies the second meaning.
explanation.definitionFit: A famous entertainer is a star, and the Daily Star is a popular British red-top newspaper.

clue.text: One may be missed in an instant

blocks.note: first meaning: a pulse that skips, as when the heart misses a beat
second meaning: a moment

explanation.surface: Something can be lost in the blink of an eye.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One may be missed' sounds like a vague bus or chance; it is the heart missing a beat from shock or excitement.
explanation.definitionFit: A heart can skip a single pulse, and doing something in a heartbeat means doing it immediately, so it stands for a moment.

clue.text: Greek punishment backed by one Conservative

indicators.note: something backed goes into reverse, so its letters run the other way

explanation.walkthrough: 'backed' looks like 'supported by', but it turns the punishment round. As in 'spare the rod', the rod means physical punishment.
explanation.definitionFit: Doric is one of the classical orders of ancient Hellenic architecture, and the dialect of the Dorians, so it is Greek.

clue.text: 24 April, so stormy

explanation.definitionFit: Polaris, the North Star or Pole Star, is the bright celestial body almost directly above the north pole.

clue.text: Majestic gallery with cunning exterior

explanation.surface: An imposing art gallery hiding behind a deceptive façade.
explanation.walkthrough: The Tate is the group of British national art galleries, Tate Britain and Tate Modern in London; it sits inside the word for crafty.
explanation.definitionFit: Stately describes grand, dignified bearing or buildings, as in a stately home, so it matches regal and imposing.
